The report, based on data from the U.S. Census Bureau's American Community Survey, defines children in poverty as those under the age of 18, living in families with annual incomes below $23,624.

That's what you call poverty? That's a shit ton of money. I understand that there's a difference between states, with e.g. California is way more expensive than, say, Kentucky, but as far as I know, unless you're living in a really expensive city/state, 23600 a year is plenty for a decent, if frugal, life.

At the same time, big differences between how "expensive" various states are seem to render this statistic completely meaningless, since it seems to be using a single number to define poverty in the entire US.

I think that's a cut off maximum. I don't believe these families are sitting around with precisely $23,600 to spend. Some will be far below that. As for the ones who are at that level, I think it would be missing the point that we say "that amount is enough to live on, so we shouldn't try to improve our economy since there's nothing wrong with that". The goal of any good society is to look at its weakest links on the chain and make it stronger, rather than saying "those links aren't too rusted".

Of course, but my point is that the number is unreasonably high, and doesn't reflect differences between areas. It seems to me that the only purpose of this report is to enable UNICEF to say "See? poverty is a big problem even in the developed world! Give us money!".

And I don't think that the goal of any good society shouldn't be to make its "weakest links" stronger, only to not prevent them from doing so if they want themselves. If "the society", which largely means the government, decides to forcibly "make someone stronger", it always ends with injustice, loss of freedom, and a lot of the time with mass death.

Unreasonably high? I'm not sure. It's not like a family of 3 or 4 can live off $23,624 income (that's before taxes) and be eating caviar and lobsters. I think your definition of reasonable differs from mine. You're welcome to cynically say that an independent report on poverty is only useful to garner more money for UNICEF, because it has no other purpose since it's not helpful to you or anyone who thinks the same as you. As for me, I consider it a decent data point that is useful in a list of other data points to paint a trend of how well the economy is doing.

I also disagree with your assertion of "only to not prevent them from doing so if they want themselves". People without jobs aren't lacking the motivation to be more financially well-off, and many times they lack those jobs despite being extremely qualified. It's because some decisions made by society at large as well as local ballot measures affect jobs' presence. We know that decisions made by local, state and federal governments have massive effect on the economy at all levels.

Here's an example, my local government passed a ballot measure to increase property tax partially offsetting a payroll tax decrease. I voted for it, and it passed. Within a few years, new companies moved here because of the lower payroll tax, bringing with them jobs. The government is me, and my neighbors and we made it possible for our community to prosper.

See, here's the thing: 23624 USD a year is almost twice the average wage where I live (eastern Europe) - and I'm fairly certain that my tax burden is way bigger than yours. On top of that, everything except services costs either roughly the same (e.g. food), or significantly more (e.g. cars, gasoline, electronics) due to additional taxes. Services cost more because they depend more heavily on wages, and wages are higher in the US; goods depend less on wages and more on things like materials prices; those are determined by a (more or less) global market, so we don't get those any cheaper.

Yet still, people manage to raise children on far less than your 23624 USD a year. That's why I consider that figure heavily inflated, and that's why I consider that report to be a ploy to get more money for whoever published it (turns out it wasn't UNICEF, I misread the article).

By increasing property tax and lowering payroll tax, you attracted new companies who brought new jobs - great. You also made living more expensive for everyone who didn't benefit from those new jobs; the people most hit by this are the ones who own a property but don't have a job (= don't benefit from the lower payroll tax either). That would be, for example, retired people. Did you consider that?

I wouldn't call that a shit ton of money. That's for a family, not an individual. So let's pretend your family lives in a cheap apartment, maybe 700 a month, plus enough money for heat, lights, an internet connection (which we know is not cheap in the US) so the children can learn and do homework after school, and a vehicle with insurance and gasoline. Let's pretend that somehow we managed to get all that on 1000 dollars a month total, that's over half your income gone and you haven't even fed yourselves or your children yet.
